title: They wrote it down
hook: Emanuel Ringelblum's team buries the Warsaw ghetto's records in metal boxes and milk cans

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ghettos, and your line: almost nothing to bless. Today, inside the walls of one ghetto, Warsaw, with people who would not let it be forgotten.

Rubble in a ruined city, some years after the war. A crew is digging under what's left of a building, following directions from someone who survived. A shovel strikes metal. They lift out a battered box, packed tight with paper. Later, nearby, they find milk cans, sealed shut and buried the same way. Inside: diaries, reports, posters, children's essays, ration cards, a theater ticket. The voice of a whole community, folded into tins.
screen: `A SHOVEL STRIKES METAL.` → `MILK CANS FULL OF PAPER.` → `A COMMUNITY FOLDED INTO TINS.`

segments.voice: Emanuel Ringelblum was a historian. When the Warsaw ghetto was sealed, he did what a historian does. He gathered a secret team of writers, teachers, rabbis, economists and young volunteers, and they began to collect everything. They gave their group a code name, Oneg Shabbat, Hebrew for the joy of the Sabbath, because they met on Saturdays. It sounded like a gathering to sing. It was an archive. They wrote reports on hunger and smuggling and how people were dying. They asked people to write about their lives, and children about theirs. They kept the German orders, the theater tickets, the soup kitchen menus, the scraps. When the deportations began, they packed it into metal boxes and milk cans and buried it under a school building. One of the young helpers left a note in with the papers. The gist of what he wrote: what we could not cry out to the world, we have buried in the ground. Part of the archive was dug up after the war. Part has never been found. Ringelblum himself did not survive. The Tanakh itself cares about writing things down, so they can be read later by people who were not there. Job, in his suffering, cries out: "Oh that my words were now written!" Not saved. Not explained. Just written, so that someone will know. That was the quiet resistance of Oneg Shabbat. They could not stop what was happening. They could make sure it could not be denied.
screen: `A HISTORIAN AND A SECRET TEAM.` · `ONEG SHABBAT: THE JOY OF THE SABBATH.` · `BURIED IN BOXES AND MILK CANS.` · `PART FOUND, PART STILL LOST.` · then, large: `OH THAT MY WORDS WERE NOW WRITTEN.`

segments.voice: Look back over the last day and let one true thing rise: something you saw, something someone said, something you did that you'd rather not have, something kind that nobody noticed. Don't polish it; hold it in plain words, just as it was.
Oneg Shabbat. The code name, Hebrew for the joy of the Sabbath, for Emanuel Ringelblum's secret team that recorded and buried the Warsaw ghetto's story. Today's word.
Your line: it could not be denied. A whole community kept its own record. That's day one thousand twelve.

howItsDone: The Oneg Shabbat archive is kept and studied today, and Jewish communities read from ghetto diaries and testimonies at Holocaust memorial gatherings so the record is heard aloud.
